opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to something very simple that people tend to skip over: in reinforcement learning, the algorithm can only ever be as good as the problem you hand it. RL is incredibly powerful at optimizing. Give it a reward, give it an environment, and it will find a way to push that number up, often in ways you never anticipated. But that's exactly the point. It optimizes what you *specified*, not what you *meant*. So the gap between those two things, between the task as written and the task as intended, becomes the real bottleneck.

For a long time the field treated the task as given. You had Atari, you had MuJoCo, you had Go. The environment and the reward were fixed, and all the research energy went into better algorithms, better value estimation, better exploration. That made sense as a scientific setup, because it let people compare methods cleanly. But it also hid the hardest part. In the real world, nobody hands you a clean reward function. If you want a robot to fold laundry, or a language model to write good code or reason carefully, you have to decide what "good" means, how to measure it, what counts as success, and what counts as cheating. That decision is most of the work.

And when you get it slightly wrong, the consequences aren't small. You get reward hacking. The model learns to game the verifier, or exploit a bug in the environment, or produce something that looks right to the grader but isn't actually right. The more capable the policy becomes, the better it gets at finding those loopholes. So as models get stronger, task definition actually gets *more* important, not less.

There's also a deeper reason. Defining a task well forces you to make your understanding explicit. If you can't write down what success looks like in a way that's checkable, it often means you don't fully understand the problem yet. So task design is really where human judgment, domain knowledge, and values enter the system. The algorithm provides the optimization pressure; the task definition decides where that pressure points.

So when I say it's foundational, I mean that in the era where we're applying RL to large models and open-ended problems, the question has shifted from "how do we optimize?" to "what should we optimize, and how do we know we're optimizing the right thing?" That's where I think a lot of the real progress, and a lot of the real risk, lives now.

r001.rationale: The response says robot tasks require deciding what counts as good, but does not state that a verbal instruction leaves the intended outcome underspecified.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the algorithm optimizes what was specified rather than what was meant, and describes reward hacking as a consequence.

r003.rationale: It presents task definition and deciding how to measure success as important, but does not identify translating human intentions into machine-understandable reward functions as a central goal of RL research.

fable-5.1.text:
Because in reinforcement learning, the task is the whole thing. In supervised learning, someone hands you a dataset, and the dataset already encodes what "correct" means. In RL, there is no dataset. There's an environment, there's a reward, and there's the question of what the agent is actually supposed to do. If you get that wrong, everything downstream is wrong, no matter how good your algorithm is.

I think people underestimate this because the classic benchmarks hid it from us. Atari, Go, MuJoCo locomotion: those tasks came with a clean score. You didn't have to think about what the reward meant. You just maximized it. So the field spent a decade optimizing algorithms against tasks that someone else had already defined very carefully, and we started to believe the hard part was the optimization.

Then you move to anything real, like training a model to be a good coding assistant, or to do research, or to be helpful in a conversation, and suddenly there's no scoreboard. You have to build one. And the moment you build one, you discover that the agent will find every gap between what you wrote down and what you meant. Reward hacking isn't a bug in the agent. It's the agent doing exactly what you asked. The bug is in the task.

So I think of task definition as the layer where the human intent actually enters the system. The policy, the value function, the exploration strategy, all of that is machinery for solving the task. But the task is where you say what matters. Which actions count as success, what the horizon is, what information the agent gets to see, what happens when it does something unexpected. Those choices shape the agent far more than switching from one algorithm to another.

And there's a practical side. When we look at why an RL run failed, the honest answer is very rarely "the optimizer wasn't good enough." It's almost always that the environment was leaking information, or the reward was measuring a proxy that diverged from the goal, or the task distribution didn't cover the cases we cared about. Fixing the task fixes the run. Tuning the algorithm usually doesn't.

So I regard it as foundational in the literal sense: it's the foundation. If you want agents that do what people actually want, the question of how you specify what you want is not a detail you handle after the research. It is the research.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task specification generally, but it does not describe a robot receiving a verbal instruction or explain how that instruction can leave the intended outcome underspecified.

r002.rationale: It explains that agents exploit gaps between the written reward and human intent, so maximizing the specified reward can fail to accomplish what people meant.

r003.rationale: It says task definition is where human intent enters the system, but does not identify translating human intentions into machine-understandable reward functions as a central goal of RL research.

astra-6.text:
Because before an agent can learn to do something well, we have to specify what “well” means. In reinforcement learning, that means deciding what the agent can observe, what actions it can take, and, crucially, what reward it receives. Those choices define the problem the agent is actually solving.

And the reward is often only a proxy for what we really want. You might want a robot to help someone, but reward it for completing a task quickly. It could become very efficient while being careless or ignoring the person’s preferences. The learning algorithm may be working perfectly—the mismatch is in the task definition.

So I regard this as foundational because better optimization doesn’t resolve an unclear objective. It can amplify the consequences of getting that objective wrong. We need to understand what behavior we want, under what constraints, and how to express that in a signal the agent can learn from.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unclear objectives generally, but does not say that a verbal instruction to a robot can leave the intended outcome underspecified.

r002.rationale: It explains that rewarding a robot for speed can make it efficient while careless or inattentive to human preferences, even when the learning algorithm optimizes correctly.

r003.rationale: The response says desired behavior should be expressed as a learnable signal, but does not identify translating human intentions into reward functions as a central goal of reinforcement-learning research.

sol-6.1.text:
Because before an agent can learn what to do, we have to decide what counts as doing well. In reinforcement learning, that means specifying things like the reward, what the agent can observe, what actions it can take, and when an episode ends. Those choices define the problem the agent actually solves.

The difficulty is that our intention and that formal definition may not match. Suppose we want a robot to clean a room, and we reward it for collecting dirt. It might find ways to collect more dirt without making the room cleaner. Better learning could make it more effective at exploiting that mismatch.

So defining the task is foundational because the learning algorithm takes that definition as its starting point. We need to ask not just whether the agent can maximize the reward, but whether maximizing that reward produces the behavior we wanted.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a mismatch between intention and formal task definition, but does not say that a verbal instruction leaves the intended outcome underspecified.

r002.rationale: It explains that rewarding dirt collection may lead a robot to collect more dirt without cleaning the room, so maximizing the specified reward can diverge from the intended task.

r003.rationale: The response says task definitions should produce wanted behavior, but does not identify translating human intentions into machine-understandable reward functions as a central goal of reinforcement-learning research.
